<style>
  :root{
    --bg:#0f1218; --panel:#161b24; --panel2:#1c2230;
    --ink:#e8ecf1; --mute:#9aa4b2; --line:#2a3242;
    --yellow:#ffd866; --blue:#58c4dd; --green:#83c167;
    --pink:#e07a5f; --violet:#b39ddb; --cyan:#7de0d6;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  html,body{margin:0;padding:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
    font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Inter,Roboto,sans-serif;
    font-size:17px;line-height:1.65}
  a{color:var(--blue)}
  code{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;
    background:#0b0f16;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:4px;color:#f0c987;font-size:0.92em}
  main{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;padding:4rem 1.5rem 8rem}
  h1{font-size:2.4rem;letter-spacing:-0.01em;margin:0 0 0.4rem}
  h2{font-size:1.6rem;margin:3.2rem 0 0.8rem;color:#fff;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding-bottom:.4rem}
  h3{font-size:1.15rem;margin:1.8rem 0 .6rem;color:var(--yellow)}
  p{margin:0.7rem 0}
  .sub{color:var(--mute);margin-top:0;margin-bottom:2rem}
  .widget{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px;
    padding:1rem 1.1rem 1.2rem;margin:1.2rem 0}
  .widget .hd{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;margin-bottom:.6rem;gap:.8rem;flex-wrap:wrap}
  .widget .hd .ttl{font-weight:600;color:#fff;font-size:.95rem;letter-spacing:.02em;text-transform:uppercase}
  .widget .hd .hint{color:var(--mute);font-size:.85rem}
  .row{display:flex;gap:.6rem;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;margin:.4rem 0}
  .row label{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem}
  input[type="text"],input[type="number"],select{
    background:#0b0f16;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .55rem;font-family:inherit;font-size:.95rem}
  input[type="range"]{accent-color:var(--yellow);flex:1;max-width:260px}
  button{background:var(--panel2);color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .7rem;cursor:pointer;font:inherit}
  button:hover{background:#242c3e}
  button.active{background:var(--yellow);color:#111;border-color:var(--yellow)}
  .readout{background:#0b0f16;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:6px;
    padding:.6rem .8rem;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:.92rem;color:#cbd5e1;
    min-height:1.6em;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word}
  .pill{display:inline-block;background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:999px;padding:1px 8px;font-size:.82rem;color:var(--mute);margin-right:4px}
  .note{border-left:3px solid var(--violet);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d8d2ef;background:#1a1828;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .ok{border-left:3px solid var(--green);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d5ebc8;background:#1a2418;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .bad{border-left:3px solid var(--pink);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#f4d2c7;background:#2a1a18;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  svg{display:block;margin:0 auto;max-width:100%}
  svg text{fill:var(--ink);font-family:inherit}
  nav.toc{position:sticky;top:0;background:rgba(15,18,24,.93);backdrop-filter:blur(8px);
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding:.6rem 1rem;z-index:10;
    display:flex;gap:1rem;flex-wrap:wrap;font-size:.9rem}
  nav.toc a{color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none}
  nav.toc a:hover{color:var(--yellow)}
  /* sticky sidebar TOC (wide screens only; narrow screens fall back to top-nav) */
  aside.sidetoc{position:fixed;top:4.2rem;
    left:max(1rem, calc(50% - 440px - 220px));
    width:200px;max-height:calc(100vh - 6rem);overflow-y:auto;
    padding-right:1rem;border-right:1px solid var(--line);
    font-size:.88rem;z-index:5}
  aside.sidetoc .sidetoc-title{font-size:.7rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute);margin:0 0 .5rem;padding-bottom:.35rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line)}
  aside.sidetoc ol{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc li{margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc a{display:block;padding:.3rem .5rem;color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none;
    border-left:2px solid transparent;line-height:1.35;
    transition:color 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease}
  aside.sidetoc a:hover{color:var(--ink)}
  aside.sidetoc a.active{color:var(--yellow);border-left-color:var(--yellow)}
  @media (max-width:1180px){ aside.sidetoc{display:none} }
  @media (min-width:1181px){ nav.toc a[href^="#"]{display:none} }
  .hero{padding:3rem 0 1rem}
  .small{font-size:.88rem;color:var(--mute)}
  footer{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem;text-align:center;margin-top:4rem}
  table.plain{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:.95rem;margin:.6rem 0}
  table.plain th,table.plain td{padding:.35rem .5rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);text-align:left}
  table.plain th{color:var(--mute);font-weight:500}
  /* callback-css-auto-begin */
  aside.callback{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:rgba(88,196,221,0.05);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--cyan) 45%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.callback .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.callback ul{margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem}
  aside.callback ul li{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.callback a{color:inherit}
/* callback-css-auto-end */
  details.changelog{
    margin:2rem 0 1rem;padding:.6rem .9rem;
    background:rgba(0,0,0,0.22);
    border-radius:6px;
    font-size:.85rem;
  }
  details.changelog summary{
    cursor:pointer;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;
    font-size:.7rem;color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);
  }
  details.changelog table{margin-top:.5rem;border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:.82rem}
  details.changelog td{padding:.2rem .6rem;border-bottom:1px dashed rgba(255,255,255,0.07);vertical-align:top}
  details.changelog td:first-child{color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);white-space:nowrap;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  aside.related{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 6%, transparent);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 55%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.related .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.related > div{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.related .more{color:var(--mute);font-style:italic}
  aside.related a{color:inherit}
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-begin */
  html[data-hide-widgets] .widget { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-quizzes] .quiz { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-lineage] .lineage-strip { display: none !important; }
  .mv-display-toggles { display: inline-flex; gap: .6rem; align-items: center; }
  .mv-display-toggle { background: transparent; border: 1px solid var(--line, #333); border-radius: 6px; padding: 5px 10px; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1.05rem; line-height: 1; color: inherit; transition: background 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease; }
  .mv-display-toggle:hover { background: var(--panel, rgba(255,255,255,0.06)); border-color: var(--mute, #666); }
  .mv-display-toggle--off { opacity: 0.35; }
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-end */
</style>

Cobordism

Two closed manifolds are cobordant when they jointly bound a manifold one dimension up. Cobordism turns "is $M$ the boundary of something?" into a graded ring whose answers are computed by characteristic numbers, the Thom spectrum, and — in the modern reading — a category whose functors are topological field theories.

Reader's note. This page assumes comfort with smooth manifolds, with characteristic classes (especially Stiefel–Whitney and Pontryagin), and with a first acquaintance with handle decompositions from Morse theory §2. It shows how the bordism relation organises all of these into a single ring-theoretic / homotopical / category-theoretic object — the gateway from differential topology into stable homotopy and TQFT.

blocks.html:
1. Cobordism as an equivalence relation

Let $M_0,M_1$ be closed (compact, no boundary) smooth $n$-manifolds. They are cobordant, written $M_0\sim M_1$, when there is a compact smooth $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ — a cobordism — with

$\partial W \;=\; M_0\sqcup M_1.$

Reflexivity uses the cylinder $M\times[0,1]$; symmetry flips the two ends; transitivity glues two cobordisms along their shared boundary using a collar neighbourhood. The set of equivalence classes of closed $n$-manifolds is denoted $\Omega_n^{O}$ ("$O$" for "unoriented", referring to the structure group of the tangent bundle).

The graded ring structure

Disjoint union makes $\Omega_n^{O}$ an abelian group: $[M]+[M']=[M\sqcup M']$, with identity $[\emptyset]$. The relation $[M]+[M]=0$ holds because $M\sqcup M = \partial(M\times[0,1])$ — every class is its own additive inverse, so $\Omega_*^{O}$ is a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Cartesian product gives a multiplication $[M]\cdot[M']=[M\times M']$, making $\Omega_*^{O}=\bigoplus_n\Omega_n^{O}$ a graded-commutative $\mathbb{F}_2$-algebra.

Why $\partial W = M_0\sqcup M_1$ and not $M_0\sqcup -M_1$? In the unoriented setting there is no notion of orientation reversal, so disjoint union is the only operation available. In the oriented bordism ring $\Omega_*^{SO}$ one demands $\partial W = M_0\sqcup\overline{M_1}$ (with $M_1$'s orientation reversed) — that is what makes $[M]+[\overline M]=0$ instead of $[M]+[M]=0$, so $\Omega_*^{SO}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-algebra rather than an $\mathbb{F}_2$-algebra.

Worked examples in low dimension

Dimension 0. A closed $0$-manifold is a finite set of points, classified up to cobordism by its parity: $\Omega_0^{O}=\mathbb{Z}/2$, generated by $[\mathrm{pt}]$. Two points are null-cobordant via the interval; one point is not.

Dimension 1. Every closed $1$-manifold is a disjoint union of circles, and every $S^1$ bounds the disk $D^2$. So $\Omega_1^{O}=0$.

Dimension 2. Every closed orientable surface $\Sigma_g$ is the boundary of a handlebody (the standard genus-$g$ solid). The Klein bottle $K$ bounds the twisted $I$-bundle over $S^1$. The real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$, however, does not bound: the unique non-trivial Stiefel–Whitney number $w_1^2\ne 0$ obstructs (next section). So $\Omega_2^{O}=\mathbb{Z}/2$, generated by $[\mathbb{RP}^2]$.

2. Stiefel–Whitney and Pontryagin numbers as obstructions

How do we tell whether a manifold bounds? The first answer is characteristic numbers: integers (or $\mathbb{F}_2$-elements) extracted by pairing characteristic classes of $TM$ against the fundamental class $[M]$.

Stiefel–Whitney numbers

Let $M^n$ be a closed manifold and $w_i = w_i(TM) \in H^i(M;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ its Stiefel–Whitney classes. For each partition $i_1+\cdots+i_r=n$, the Stiefel–Whitney number is

$w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_r}[M] \;:=\; \langle w_{i_1}\smile\cdots\smile w_{i_r},\;[M]_{\mathbb{Z}/2}\rangle \;\in\;\mathbb{Z}/2.$

where $[M]_{\mathbb{Z}/2}\in H_n(M;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is the mod-2 fundamental class (which always exists, oriented or not).

Why these are cobordism invariants. If $\partial W = M$, then $TW|_M = TM\oplus\nu$ where $\nu$ is the rank-1 outward-normal bundle. Since $\nu$ is trivial near the boundary, $w(TM) = w(TW|_M)$. By naturality $w_i(TW|_M) = j^* w_i(TW)$ where $j\colon M\hookrightarrow W$. Then $\langle w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_r}(TM),[M]\rangle = \langle j^*(w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_r}(TW)),[M]\rangle = \langle w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_r}(TW),j_*[M]\rangle = 0$, because $j_*[M]=\partial[W]=0$ in $H_n(W;\mathbb{Z}/2)$. So every SW number of $M$ vanishes whenever $M$ bounds.

The converse: Thom's theorem (1954)

The astonishing fact is that Stiefel–Whitney numbers are a complete invariant of unoriented bordism:

$M$ is null-cobordant in $\Omega_*^{O}$ $\iff$ every Stiefel–Whitney number of $M$ vanishes.

Equivalently, two closed manifolds are cobordant iff all their SW numbers agree. So $\Omega_*^{O}\hookrightarrow\prod\mathbb{Z}/2$ via SW numbers is an injection — and Thom showed it determines the entire ring.

Worked example: $\mathbb{RP}^2$ does not bound

The total Stiefel–Whitney class of $T\mathbb{RP}^n$ is $w(T\mathbb{RP}^n) = (1+a)^{n+1}$ in $H^*(\mathbb{RP}^n;\mathbb{Z}/2)=\mathbb{Z}/2[a]/(a^{n+1})$ with $|a|=1$. For $n=2$, $w(T\mathbb{RP}^2) = (1+a)^3 = 1 + a + a^2$, so $w_1 = a$ and $w_2 = a^2$.

The single SW number in dimension 2 with one $w_2$ and one with $w_1^2$:

$\langle w_1^2,[\mathbb{RP}^2]\rangle = \langle a^2,[\mathbb{RP}^2]\rangle = 1\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}/2,\qquad \langle w_2,[\mathbb{RP}^2]\rangle = 1.$

Either non-zero number is enough to obstruct boundedness. Contrast with $S^2$: $w(TS^2) = 1$ (the tangent bundle is stably trivial), so all SW numbers vanish — and indeed $S^2 = \partial D^3$.

Pontryagin numbers (oriented case)

For an oriented $M^{4k}$, the Pontryagin classes $p_i(TM)\in H^{4i}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ pair against $[M]\in H_{4k}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ to give integer Pontryagin numbers $p_{i_1}\cdots p_{i_r}[M]$ for partitions $i_1+\cdots+i_r=k$. By the same boundary-vs-fundamental-class argument, Pontryagin numbers vanish on boundaries.

Combined with SW numbers, they give the full obstruction in the oriented case:

$[M]=0$ in $\Omega_*^{SO}$ $\iff$ every SW number AND every Pontryagin number vanishes.

The top SW number $\langle w_n,[\mathbb{RP}^n]\rangle = \binom{n+1}{n}\bmod 2 = (n+1)\bmod 2$. 3. Thom's theorem and the Thom spectrum $MO$

Pontryagin's converse — that SW numbers see everything — is not proved by checking cases. It is proved by recasting the entire bordism ring as the homotopy of a single space (a spectrum), the Thom spectrum $MO$.

The Pontryagin–Thom construction

Given a closed $n$-manifold $M$, embed $M\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$ for $k$ large (Whitney). Let $\nu\to M$ be the rank-$k$ normal bundle, and $D(\nu)\to M$ its disk bundle, with sphere bundle $S(\nu)\subset D(\nu)$. The tubular neighbourhood theorem gives an embedding $D(\nu)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n+k}$. Now collapse everything outside $D(\nu)$ to a point: the result is the Thom space $$T(\nu) \;=\; D(\nu)/S(\nu),$$ and the construction gives a map $$S^{n+k} = \mathbb{R}^{n+k}\cup\{\infty\}\;\xrightarrow{\;\;c\;\;}\;T(\nu)\xrightarrow{\;\;}\;T(\gamma_k^{O(k)})\;=:\;MO(k),$$ where $\gamma_k^{O(k)}$ is the universal rank-$k$ real bundle over $BO(k)$. The composite is a class in $\pi_{n+k}(MO(k))$.

Stabilising in $k$ (Thom spaces of trivial extensions) gives a class in $\pi_n(MO)$, where $MO$ is the spectrum with $k$-th space $MO(k)$.

Theorem (Thom, 1954). The Pontryagin–Thom construction induces an isomorphism of graded rings $$\Omega_*^{O} \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\pi_*(MO).$$ The reverse map sends a homotopy class $f\colon S^{n+k}\to MO(k)$ to the preimage $f^{-1}(BO(k))$, made transverse — this preimage is a closed $n$-submanifold of $S^{n+k}$.

Thom's calculation of $\pi_*(MO)$

Using mod-2 cohomology and the Steenrod algebra, Thom computed

$\pi_*(MO) \;\cong\; \mathbb{F}_2[x_i \;:\; i\ge 1,\;i\ne 2^k-1] \;=\; \mathbb{F}_2[x_2,x_4,x_5,x_6,x_8,x_9,\ldots],$

a polynomial $\mathbb{F}_2$-algebra on generators in every degree except $1,3,7,15,\ldots$ (the Mersenne degrees). Generators in even degree $2k$ can be taken to be $[\mathbb{RP}^{2k}]$; generators in non-Mersenne odd degree have explicit (more complicated) representatives, the Dold manifolds.

4. Oriented cobordism and the signature theorem

Restricting to oriented manifolds and oriented cobordisms produces a finer invariant: the oriented bordism ring $\Omega_*^{SO}$. Now $[M]+[\overline{M}]=0$ rather than $2[M]=0$, so $\Omega_*^{SO}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-algebra; the Pontryagin–Thom construction gives $\Omega_*^{SO}\cong\pi_*(MSO)$ where $MSO$ is the Thom spectrum of $BSO$.

Rational structure

The integral ring $\Omega_*^{SO}$ has 2-torsion (coming from $\mathbb{F}_2$-style obstructions left over from $\Omega_*^{O}$), but it becomes very clean rationally:

$\Omega_*^{SO}\otimes\mathbb{Q} \;\cong\; \mathbb{Q}[\mathbb{CP}^2,\mathbb{CP}^4,\mathbb{CP}^6,\ldots],$

a polynomial ring on the even-complex-dimensional projective spaces. (Why even? Because $\mathbb{CP}^{2k+1}$ admits an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism, so $[\mathbb{CP}^{2k+1}]=-[\mathbb{CP}^{2k+1}]$ in $\Omega_*^{SO}\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, hence vanishes.) So $\Omega_n^{SO}\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is non-zero precisely when $n\equiv 0\pmod 4$, with rank equal to the number of partitions of $n/4$.

The signature ring homomorphism

For a closed oriented $4k$-manifold $M$, the cup-product pairing $H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{R})\otimes H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}$, $\alpha\otimes\beta\mapsto\langle\alpha\smile\beta,[M]\rangle$, is a symmetric non-degenerate form (Poincaré duality, see Cohomology and duality §3). Its signature $\sigma(M)$ is the dimension of the maximal positive-definite subspace minus the dimension of the maximal negative-definite subspace. Set $\sigma(M)=0$ in dimensions not divisible by 4.

Signature is additive over disjoint union, multiplicative over Cartesian product (Novikov), and vanishes on boundaries (Thom). So it descends to a graded-ring homomorphism

$\sigma\colon \Omega_*^{SO}\to\mathbb{Z}.$

Hirzebruch's signature theorem

The Hirzebruch theorem identifies $\sigma$ as a Pontryagin number. Define the multiplicative $L$-genus in Pontryagin classes via the formal series $\prod_i \tfrac{x_i}{\tanh x_i}$:

$L_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}p_1,\qquad L_2 = \tfrac{1}{45}(7p_2 - p_1^2),\qquad L_3 = \tfrac{1}{945}(62p_3 - 13p_2p_1 + 2p_1^3),\quad\ldots$

The Hirzebruch signature theorem (1954) says: for a closed oriented $M^{4k}$,

$\sigma(M) \;=\; \langle L_k(p_1,\ldots,p_k),[M]\rangle.$

So a quantity built from cup products of cohomology classes (signature) equals an explicit polynomial in Pontryagin classes (curvature data of the tangent bundle). This is the prototype of an index theorem — both the topological index of an elliptic operator (here, $d+d^*$ on even forms) and the analytic index (the signature) are computed by the same characteristic-class formula.

Worked example: $\sigma(\mathbb{CP}^2) = 1$. $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}\cdot x$ with $\langle x^2,[\mathbb{CP}^2]\rangle = 1$, so the form is the rank-one $(1)$, signature $1$. On the Pontryagin side, $T\mathbb{CP}^2$ has $p_1 = 3x^2$, so $L_1[\mathbb{CP}^2] = \tfrac{1}{3}\langle p_1,[\mathbb{CP}^2]\rangle = \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot 3 = 1$. The two sides agree — the signature theorem in degree 4. Iterating: $\sigma(\mathbb{CP}^{2k})=1$ in every dimension $4k$, which is exactly what makes $[\mathbb{CP}^{2k}]$ a polynomial generator of $\Omega_*^{SO}\otimes\mathbb{Q}$.

5. Surgery and the $h$-cobordism theorem

So far we have used cobordism as an equivalence relation and computed the bordism ring. The other side of the story is using cobordism to do work: to manipulate manifolds within their bordism class via surgery, and ultimately — when the cobordism is an $h$-cobordism — to conclude that the two ends are diffeomorphic.

Surgery

Let $M^n$ be a closed $n$-manifold and suppose we have an embedding

$\varphi\colon S^p\times D^q \;\hookrightarrow\; M, \qquad p+q=n.$

Surgery along $\varphi$ produces a new manifold $M'$ by removing the embedded $S^p\times D^q$ and gluing in $D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}$ along the common boundary $S^p\times S^{q-1}$:

$M' \;=\; \bigl(M\setminus\mathrm{int}\,\varphi(S^p\times D^q)\bigr) \;\cup_{S^p\times S^{q-1}}\; D^{p+1}\times S^{q-1}.$

The trace of the surgery is the cobordism

$W = M\times[0,1]\;\cup_\varphi\;D^{p+1}\times D^q,$

obtained by attaching a $(p+1)$-handle to the cylinder $M\times[0,1]$ along $\varphi$. Then $\partial W = M\sqcup M'$, so $M$ and $M'$ are cobordant — in fact $M$ and $M'$ differ by exactly one handle, a localised modification.

Connection to Morse theory. A $(p+1)$-handle is glued exactly when crossing a Morse critical value of index $p+1$ in the cobordism (see Morse theory §2). So every cobordism between closed $M_0,M_1$ admits a handle decomposition, and you can equivalently move $M_0$ to $M_1$ by a sequence of surgeries. Surgery is the "operational" face of cobordism.

$h$-cobordisms

A cobordism $W$ between $M_0$ and $M_1$ is an $h$-cobordism when both inclusions $M_0\hookrightarrow W$ and $M_1\hookrightarrow W$ are homotopy equivalences. Cylinders $M\times[0,1]$ are obvious examples; the question is whether any others exist.

The $h$-cobordism theorem (Smale, 1962)

Theorem. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $h$-cobordism between closed simply-connected manifolds $M_0$ and $M_1$, with $\dim W \ge 6$. Then $W$ is diffeomorphic to $M_0\times[0,1]$. In particular $M_0\cong M_1$ diffeomorphically.

The proof works by Cerf-theoretic handle cancellation (see Morse theory §8): start with a Morse function on $W$, eliminate $0$- and $n$-handles by killing critical points using simple connectivity, then cancel pairs of adjacent-index handles using the Whitney trick — sliding handles past each other in a $(p,q)$-disk pair. The Whitney trick needs $\dim W \ge 5$ to embed the disk pair without self-intersection, and the dimension constraint $\ge 6$ comes from a margin in the indexing.

The dimension hypothesis is sharp. The theorem is false in dimension $4$: Donaldson and Freedman gave examples of $h$-cobordant smooth $4$-manifolds that are not diffeomorphic. The Whitney trick fails — there is no room to embed the disks transversally — and exotic smooth structures proliferate. This is one face of why dimension $4$ is the hardest: smooth and topological categories diverge.

Consequences

  • The Poincaré conjecture in dim $\ge 5$. If $\Sigma^n$ ($n\ge 5$) is a homotopy $n$-sphere, then $\Sigma\setminus(\text{open ball})$ is an $h$-cobordism between $\partial(\text{ball})=S^{n-1}$ and itself, so it is a cylinder, so $\Sigma$ is a sphere. (This is Smale's celebrated 1961 proof, in the smooth/PL category. Stallings and Zeeman gave PL proofs around the same time. The topological case in dimensions $\ge 5$ was settled later by Newman 1966; dim 4 topological is Freedman 1982.)
  • Exotic spheres exist. Milnor's $7$-spheres are smooth manifolds homeomorphic to $S^7$ but not diffeomorphic — the smooth $h$-cobordism conclusion holds, but there is more than one diffeomorphism class compatible with a given homeomorphism class. (Kervaire–Milnor classified all of them via the group $\Theta_n$ of exotic $n$-spheres.)
  • The $s$-cobordism theorem. Dropping simple connectivity, there is an obstruction — the Whitehead torsion $\tau(W)\in\mathrm{Wh}(\pi_1)$ — and the conclusion is "trivial cobordism" iff $\tau(W)=0$. The Whitehead group is non-trivial in general (e.g. $\mathrm{Wh}(\mathbb{Z}/5) = \mathbb{Z}$), so non-cylinder $h$-cobordisms genuinely exist.

6. TQFT and the cobordism category

The most modern way to read cobordism is through Atiyah's framework of topological quantum field theories: package the entire bordism world into a single category and study its functors.

The cobordism category $\mathrm{Cob}_d$

Fix a dimension $d\ge 1$. Define a category $\mathrm{Cob}_d$:

  • Objects are closed oriented $(d-1)$-manifolds.
  • Morphisms from $\Sigma_0$ to $\Sigma_1$ are diffeomorphism classes of cobordisms $W$ with $\partial W = \overline{\Sigma_0}\sqcup\Sigma_1$ (the orientation reversal on the incoming end is the source/target convention).
  • Composition is gluing along common boundaries, identity is the cylinder $\Sigma\times[0,1]$.
  • Disjoint union is a symmetric monoidal product, with unit the empty manifold $\emptyset$.

Atiyah's axioms

A $d$-dimensional topological quantum field theory over a field $k$ is a symmetric monoidal functor

$Z\colon\mathrm{Cob}_d\;\longrightarrow\;\mathrm{Vect}_k.$

Unpacking:

  • $Z$ assigns to each closed oriented $(d-1)$-manifold $\Sigma$ a finite-dimensional vector space $Z(\Sigma)$ — the state space.
  • $Z$ assigns to each cobordism $W\colon\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ a linear map $Z(W)\colon Z(\Sigma_0)\to Z(\Sigma_1)$ — the transition amplitude.
  • $Z(\emptyset) = k$ (the monoidal unit goes to the unit), and $Z(\Sigma_0\sqcup\Sigma_1) = Z(\Sigma_0)\otimes Z(\Sigma_1)$ (disjoint union to tensor product).
  • For a closed $d$-manifold $M$, viewed as a cobordism $\emptyset\to\emptyset$, $Z(M)\in\mathrm{Hom}_k(k,k) = k$ — the partition function.

The 2D classification

Atiyah's framework already pays off in the lowest interesting dimension. A theorem of Dijkgraaf (1989, with Abrams' modern proof) says

$\{$2D TQFTs over $k\}$ $\;\;\xleftrightarrow{\;\;\sim\;\;}\;\;$ $\{$commutative Frobenius algebras over $k\}$.

The vector space is $A = Z(S^1)$, the multiplication is $Z(\text{pants})$, the trace pairing is $Z(\text{torus minus disk})$ — every algebraic axiom of a Frobenius algebra is forced by the topology of $\mathrm{Cob}_2$. Examples: group algebras of finite groups (giving 2D Dijkgraaf–Witten theory), the cohomology ring of a closed oriented manifold (Poincaré duality is the Frobenius pairing), the Jacobian ring of an isolated hypersurface singularity (Saito, Landau–Ginzburg).

Higher dimensions and full extension

In dimensions $d\ge 3$ the analogous classifications get harder (no closed-form list), and a more powerful framework is needed: fully extended TQFTs, which assign data to manifolds of every codimension from $0$ down to $d$. The objects of dimension $0$ — points — are then assigned objects in a higher category $\mathcal{C}$.

The cobordism hypothesis (Baez–Dolan, 1995; proved by Lurie, 2009). The category $\mathrm{Bord}_d^{fr}$ of fully extended framed cobordisms is the free symmetric monoidal $(\infty,d)$-category generated by a single fully dualizable object — the framed point. So fully extended framed $d$-TQFTs valued in any symmetric monoidal $(\infty,d)$-category $\mathcal{C}$ are classified by: $$\{\text{fully extended framed } d\text{-TQFTs valued in }\mathcal{C}\}\;\xleftrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\{\text{fully dualizable objects of }\mathcal{C}\},$$ via $Z\mapsto Z(\mathrm{pt})$. Adding tangential structure (orientation, spin, ...) corresponds to taking homotopy fixed points of an $O(d)$-action on the space of fully dualizable objects.

This is the deepest statement in modern cobordism theory: the entire structure of $\mathrm{Bord}_d$, with its symmetric monoidal $(\infty,d)$-category structure, is determined by what one fully dualizable object can do. It rephrases topology as a universal property in higher category theory — and ties back to $\infty$-categories and $\infty$-topoi.

Connections

Cobordism is a hub topic: it feeds the Thom-spectrum side of stable homotopy, the index-theoretic side of differential geometry, the Whitney-trick side of high-dimensional manifold theory, and the categorical side of TQFT. Open frontiers cluster around dimension $4$ (where the smooth $h$-cobordism theorem fails and almost everything is hard), the cobordism hypothesis in low dimensions (where extended TQFTs encode invariants like the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev $3$-manifold invariants), and refinements via tangential structures (Spin, String, framed) used to construct field theories on physical interest.

  • Characteristic classes — Stiefel–Whitney classes — the SW numbers of §2 are the entire obstruction to unoriented null-cobordism, and Pontryagin numbers are the rest in the oriented case.
  • Morse theory — handle decomposition — every cobordism is a sequence of handle attachments, so surgery and Morse data are two views of the same manifold.
  • K-theory — Bott periodicity — Bott periodicity gives $KU$ a similar spectrum-of-bundles structure to $MU$, and the Atiyah–Singer index theorem (a descendant of Hirzebruch's signature theorem) is computed inside both worlds.
  • Atiyah–Singer index theorem — the signature theorem of §4 is the prototype: signature = $L$-genus = analytic index of $d+d^*$ on even forms. The general index theorem upgrades this to all elliptic operators.
  • $\infty$-categories and gauge theory — the cobordism hypothesis lives in $(\infty,d)$-categories, and physically realised TQFTs (Donaldson–Floer–Seiberg–Witten on $4$-manifolds, Chern–Simons on $3$-manifolds) instantiate the framework with concrete dualizable objects.
  • Gauge theory — Donaldson invariants and Seiberg–Witten invariants are TQFT-style invariants of $4$-manifolds that detect smooth structure beyond the reach of cobordism, and explain the failure of the smooth $h$-cobordism theorem in dim 4.
